_meta.source: Protons, electrons and configurations derived from elements.json plus standard ion chemistry; average masses from the IUPAC standard atomic weights.
_meta.electronConfigurationConvention: Full configuration of the ion with subshells in ascending n then l order. Electrons are removed from the highest n first, so Fe3+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5. configPlain is the same string with ASCII digits.
_meta.polyatomicConvention: For polyatomic ions atomicNumber equals protons (the sum of the constituent atomic numbers) because a single element symbol cannot describe them. electronConfiguration and configPlain are null because a polyatomic ion has no single atomic configuration. phase is "unknown" because these ions exist only in solution.
_meta.averageMassConvention: Sum of the constituent average atomic masses minus 0.00054858 u per positive charge (electron mass).

ions.about: A bare proton, H+, is what is actually solvated in acid solutions; it makes the surrounding water molecules hydronium, H3O+.
The hydride ion, H-, is a strong base that exists in metal hydrides, in ammonia and in borohydride salts.
The lithium ion gives lithium batteries their charge; it is small enough to tunnel between layers in a solid electrode.
The sodium ion is the main cation of seawater and of blood plasma, and it gives up its electron at a sodium battery anode.
The potassium ion is essential for nerves and muscles, and it is what a potassium channel lets through the cell membrane.
The rubidium ion is a weakly coordinating anion, so its salts are used when a very unreactive counter-ion is needed.
The caesium ion is a weakly coordinating cation used to pair with very reactive anions.
Be2+ is extremely small, strongly polarising and toxic; it hydrolyses water and turns solutions acidic.
Mg2+ is the second most abundant cation in seawater and a cofactor of every ATP molecule in the body.
Ca2+ hardens water, sets the firmness of bone, and triggers muscle contraction and the clotting cascade.
Sr2+ is a heavy, water-loving cation used in fireworks and in strontium ranelate for osteoporosis.
Ba2+ is a heavy alkaline earth cation; its insoluble sulfate is safe to drink while the carbonate is a poison.
Al3+ is the hydrated cation of weakly acidic and basic solutions. Its very small radius polarises water strongly, so aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric and alumina is hard and unreactive.
Ga3+ is the stable oxidation state of gallium, and its amphoteric hydroxide dissolves in both acid and alkali.
In3+ forms stable salts in acid solution, but indium compounds should be handled with care.
The fluoride ion is the hardest anion and is a weak base; it protects teeth in toothpaste and is a trace element in the body.
The chloride ion is the counter-ion of stomach acid and the main anion of seawater; it is the active ingredient of table salt.
The bromide ion is a weaker nucleophile than chloride and is used in flame retardants and bromide photographic film.
The iodide ion is a good reducing agent, so iodide starch paper turns blue with oxidising agents.
The nitride ion, N3-, exists in magnesium nitride and in molten alkali metal nitrides; it reacts violently with water.
The oxide ion is the most common anion in the crust, forming the lattices of silicates, oxides and hydroxides.
The sulfide ion smells of rotten eggs when it is protonated, and it precipitates black metal sulfides in qualitative analysis.
The selenide ion forms in alkaline selenide solutions and precipitates metal selenides used in photocells.
The phosphide ion occurs in phosphide metals such as iron phosphide, and it is very reactive towards water.
Ti4+ is the oxidation state of titanium dioxide, the white pigment that makes paint and sunscreen opaque.
Cr2+ is a strong reducing agent in solution and is easily oxidised to the blue Cr3+ ion.
Cr3+ is the green ion of chrome alum and the oxidation state that gives ruby and emerald their colour.
Mn2+ is a pale pink ion; its permanganate oxidation state, +7, is the one that is brightly coloured.
Fe2+ is the iron in haemoglobin that carries oxygen, and it is the ion written in the iron redox chemistry of soils.
Fe3+ is the iron in haemoglobin when it is oxidised, and it is what turns rust solutions yellow-brown.
Co2+ gives pink solutions, and it is the ion used in the oxygen carrier of artificial blood substitutes.
Ni2+ is green in solution and is oxidised to Ni3+ in a nickel-cadmium cell or a nickel half-cell.
Cu+ is a soft, linear-coordinating ion that disproportionates in water to copper metal and Cu2+.
Cu2+ is the blue ion of copper sulfate; it catalyses hydrogen peroxide breakdown and gives a green flame.
Zn2+ is a d10 ion, always colourless in solution, and the active centre of hundreds of enzymes.
Ag+ is precipitated as white silver chloride or yellow silver iodide, which is why halide tests turn cloudy.
Cd2+ is a d10 ion like Zn2+ and behaves similarly, but it is far more toxic and softer.
Hg2+ is a very soft cation that binds thiol groups on proteins, which is the basis of mercury poisoning.
Sn2+ is the reducing half of the tin to Sn2+ system, used in tin plating and in the reduction of nitro compounds.
Sn4+ is the oxidising half of the same couple, and it forms the basis of the tin system in pH buffers.
Pb2+ is the toxic cation in lead water pipes and paint; it mimics calcium and accumulates in bone.
Pb4+ is a strong oxidising agent in acidic solution and is used to oxidise alcohols and carboxylic acids.
Tl3+ is a soft, strongly oxidising cation that also forms inert-pair Tl(I) compounds.

ions.name: Ammonium
ions.about: The ammonium ion, formed when ammonia dissolves in water; it is the counter-ion of almost all ammonium salts and neutralises acid in plant roots.

ions.name: Hydronium
ions.about: The hydronium ion is the real cation of any acid solution: when HCl dissolves, the proton attaches itself to a water molecule.

ions.name: Hydroxide
ions.about: The hydroxide ion is what makes alkalis alkaline. It is a strong nucleophile and a strong base.

ions.name: Nitrate
ions.about: A very stable, soluble anion. Nitrate pollution from fertiliser run-off causes algal blooms in rivers and lakes.

ions.name: Nitrite
ions.about: A reducing anion and a preservative in cured meats; it is toxic and can be written as NO in atmospheric chemistry.

ions.name: Sulfate
ions.about: The sulfate ion is one of the two common anions of natural waters and the main charge carrier in lead-acid batteries.

ions.name: Hydrogen sulfate
ions.about: Hydrogen sulfate is the acid form of sulfate, present once strong acid is added to a sulfate solution.

ions.name: Sulfite
ions.about: Sulfite is the ion that removes sulphur dioxide from flue gases; it is a mild reducing agent and bleaches dye.

ions.name: Carbonate
ions.about: The carbonate ion is the conjugate base of bicarbonate and is the main alkalinity of the ocean and of limestone.

ions.name: Bicarbonate (hydrogen carbonate)
ions.about: Bicarbonate is the buffer system that keeps blood pH near 7.4 and the main ion in baking soda.

ions.name: Phosphate
ions.about: The phosphate ion links the DNA backbone and carries energy as ATP; phosphates are the main fertiliser nutrient for plants.

ions.name: Hydrogen phosphate
ions.about: Hydrogen phosphate is the dominant phosphate species at neutral pH and is found in the phosphate buffer of biology.

ions.name: Dihydrogen phosphate
ions.about: Dihydrogen phosphate is the acidic form, used as a food acidulant and as a component of phosphate buffer solutions.

ions.name: Dihydrogen phosphite
ions.about: Phosphite is the reduced, diprotic form of phosphorous acid and is a preservative in foods and a reductant.

ions.name: Cyanide
ions.about: Cyanide is one of the fastest acting poisons, because it blocks cellular respiration by binding iron in cytochrome oxidase.

ions.name: Thiocyanate
ions.about: Thiocyanate turns blood red in the Fe3+ test, and its oxidation to thiocyanogen is used in iodine titrations.

ions.name: Chlorate
ions.about: Chlorate is a powerful oxidising agent and forms in water treatment; it is also the basis of safety matches.

ions.name: Perchlorate
ions.about: Perchlorate is a very weak base and a strong oxidiser at high temperature; it is soluble and mobile in groundwater.

ions.name: Hypochlorite
ions.about: The ion in household bleach and chlorinated pools. It bleaches because it is nucleophilic and oxidising at the same time.

ions.name: Chromate
ions.about: Chromate is yellow and turns orange dichromate when acid is added, the classic indicator colour change in titration.

ions.name: Permanganate
ions.about: Permanganate is the intense purple titrant of acid-base and redox titrations, and it is a useful test for oxidising agents.

ions.name: Acetate
ions.about: The acetate ion is the conjugate base of ethanoic acid; it buffers acetic acid solutions and is the ion in vinegar and in acetate buffers.

ions.name: Phenoxide
ions.about: Phenoxide is the ion released by phenol in base, and its sodium salt is one of the simplest aromatic nucleophiles.
